lede: Six Foundational games and Quick looks were played, read line by line, scored against research on how young children learn maths and how good learning games work, and checked against live pupil data. They are clear, friendly and use the right pictures. Four things hold them back, and all of them can be fixed.

findings.title: Mistakes teach nothing
findings.text: In every game a wrong tap gets a wobble and "Try again!". Wrong taps are free, so tapping every choice always wins, and the wrong choices are easy to rule out.

findings.title: Help follows the calendar
findings.text: In four games, pictures and labels fade by the number of days played, not by how the child is doing, and they never come back for a child who is struggling.

findings.title: Careful children can get stuck
findings.text: A fact only moves up if it is answered within 5 seconds. Slow, accurate 5-year-olds can stay on the same step, and in Hop the clock starts while the voice is still talking.

findings.title: Teachers can't see who is stuck
findings.text: Every answer is saved, but no teacher page shows who is stuck on what, and Quick looks has no teacher view at all.

findings.title: Big gaps beyond number basics
findings.text: No game yet teaches comparing numbers, equals as balance, place value past 20, equal groups, counting out a set, money, shape, measuring or graphs.

games.name: Weka's Stepping Stones
games.works: The strongest of the set. Pebbles, a number line and a hint ladder that steps in after mistakes, and help that eases off as the child does well.
games.missing: Wrong choices are only one or two away from the answer, so tapping everything still wins. The pebble step stops at ten by itself, so the child does not have to. Level 1 repeats "9 + something" a lot.
games.fix: Mistakes that teach (R5): wrong choices built from real errors like stopping at the rock, and the child decides where ten is.

games.name: Quick looks
games.idea: Subitising: seeing how many without counting
games.works: Well researched: stages in a sensible order, help comes and goes with the child, and wrong answers show the groups.
games.missing: Teachers can see nothing, although every answer is saved. "Keep the picture" practice counts towards passing, so a child can pass by counting. Reaction time is not saved.
games.fix: Quick looks fixes (R3), then put it in the teacher view (R7).

games.name: Tūī's Ten Tree
games.idea: Teen numbers as ten and some more
games.works: Excellent models: ten-frames and a kete, with help that adapts to the child.
games.missing: A bug: help never fades for a strong child until step 5, because a new step adds the help straight back. Only nine facts all term, and 14 and 41 mix-ups are never named.
games.fix: Fix the fading bug (R1), a quick win.

games.name: Pipi's Hidden Shells
games.works: The maths is the game: you really have to work out how many are hiding. A sensible order from small to bigger wholes.
games.missing: Help fades by the calendar and never comes back. A wrong tap only gets "Try again!", and tapping all four shells always wins. No "say it again" button.
games.fix: Help that follows the child (R6) and mistakes that teach (R5).

games.name: Penguin Pairs
games.works: Clear and friendly, with pictures that help early on, and the teacher can see each child's 3 hardest facts.
games.missing: On bronze days the game shares the halves out itself, so the answer can be read off. "Fair or not?" is a 50/50 guess. Only 4 short levels, ending at halves to 20.
games.fix: Mistakes that teach (R5), then a real pile for "Fair or not?" and a longer ladder (R8, R9).

games.name: Kiwi's Beanstalk
games.works: A clear goal and a lovely climb. Bonds to 100 and 1000 grow from bonds to 10.
games.missing: Random tapping can finish a day (one test day had 26 wrong taps and 8 right). The target number is only spoken, never shown. The jump from 3 + 7 to 70 + 30 has no bridge.
games.fix: Show the target and add a bridge (R4), then mistakes that teach (R5).

games.name: Hop's Glow-worm Pond
games.works: A clear, calm path, with "+10" labels as a model at first.
games.missing: Wrong choices are easy to rule out (in tens, only one ends in 0). The step-up clock starts while the voice is still talking, so careful children can get stuck on tens. Counting back comes late.
games.fix: Fair step-up for careful children (R2), then better wrong choices (R5).

ideas.title: Kererū's Number Line: reading, placing and jumping on lines to 100 and 1000
ideas.text: Place numbers on a line and find one more, one less, and where 37 goes. This is the base for place value, rounding and mental strategies.

ideas.gap: Equals as balance, and missing numbers
ideas.title: Kea's See-saw: equals means the same amount, and missing numbers
ideas.text: Make both sides weigh the same: 8 = ? + 5. It fixes the "equals means the answer comes next" mistake that blocks algebra later.

ideas.title: Tuatara's Bundles: tens and ones to 100, then hundreds
ideas.text: Bundle sticks or shells into tens and hundreds to build and read numbers. It carries on from Tūī, which stops at 20.

ideas.title: Pūkeko's Raupō Rows: equal groups and arrays, then the times tables
ideas.text: Build equal rows and groups to show what times means. The hub asks times tables more than anything else, but only as a quiz.

ideas.title: Kākāpō's Berry Basket: counting out a set, giving exactly N
ideas.text: Count out exactly the number asked for: one-to-one counting and "the last number says how many". This is the very first skill for new entrants.
